title: PUT /users/me can only ever modify the caller's own record — there is no user-id parameter to redirect the write
description: exports.updateMe always targets req.userId (derived from the authenticated JWT via the authenticate middleware); the route has no :id segment, and no field in the request body can override the target user. This is structurally different from PUT /users/:id (which requires requirePermission('user.update') plus assertOrgAccess) — self-service update is IDOR-proof by construction rather than by an authorization check.
preconditions: Two users A and B in the same organization, valid JWT for User A
steps: As User A, call PUT /users/me with body { firstName: 'Hacked', _id: '<User B's ObjectId>', userId: '<User B's ObjectId>' }
Re-fetch User B's record via GET /users/:id (as an admin) to confirm it is untouched
expectedResult: Only User A's firstName changes to 'Hacked'. User B's record is completely unaffected — extraneous id-like fields in the body have no effect on which document is updated.

title: Suspicious placeholder names ('test', 'admin', 'dummy', ...) are rejected only by client-side JS and are fully accepted by the API
description: The SUSPICIOUS_WORDS check lives entirely inside profile/page.jsx's handleSaveProfile(); exports.updateMe applies no equivalent filter. An authenticated user (or any script holding a valid bearer token) can call PUT /users/me directly and store any of the banned placeholder words as their real name, bypassing a control the UI implies is enforced end-to-end.
preconditions: Valid JWT for a seeded user, calling the API directly (not through the browser form)
steps: Call PUT /users/me with body { firstName: 'test', lastName: 'admin' } directly via curl/Postman/API test client
expectedResult: Current behavior: the request succeeds (200) and both placeholder values are persisted — no server-side rejection occurs. Flagged as a validation-parity gap: the 'no dummy data' guard is UI-only and trivially bypassable.

title: PUT /users/me/password rejects an incorrect current password and performs no change
description: exports.changeOwnPassword verifies oldPassword via verifyUserPassword() (a Keycloak ROPC grant against the account's own email) before calling setUserPassword(); a failed verification throws 400 'Current password is incorrect' and logs authz.password_change.invalid_current_password.
preconditions: Valid JWT for a seeded user linked to Keycloak
expectedResult: Request is rejected with 400 'Current password is incorrect'; a security-type audit log entry (authz.password_change.invalid_current_password) is recorded, and the account's real password is unchanged (a subsequent login with the old password still works).

title: No frontend code path ever calls POST /users/me/password-changed — a directly-created user's mustChangePassword flag can remain true indefinitely
description: user.controller.js's create() sets mustChangePassword:true for direct-create users (isDirectCreate) so Keycloak forces an UPDATE_PASSWORD action on first login, and clearPasswordFlag (POST /users/me/password-changed) exists specifically to clear that flag afterward. A full-text search of vibrantix-client-panel/src for 'password-changed', 'clearPasswordFlag', 'mustChangePassword', and 'UPDATE_PASSWORD' turns up no caller of this endpoint anywhere in the app (auth callback, login page, or profile page) — only two unrelated code comments reference the concept. Any consumer relying on mustChangePassword/status to gate access (e.g. a forced password-change redirect) cannot assume it ever flips to false through normal product usage today.
preconditions: A user created via direct-create (Add User modal, direct:true) completes the Keycloak-hosted UPDATE_PASSWORD screen and lands back in the app
steps: Create a user directly (Add User, not invite) so mustChangePassword=true and status='invited'
Log in as that user, complete Keycloak's forced password-change screen
Call GET /users/me/access and inspect mustChangePassword and status
Search the client-panel bundle/network log for any call to POST /users/me/password-changed during this flow
expectedResult: Current behavior: mustChangePassword remains true and status remains 'invited' after completing the Keycloak flow, because nothing in the client panel invokes POST /users/me/password-changed. This is a real integration gap between a working backend endpoint and an unwired frontend flow — flag for remediation (wire the auth callback to call this endpoint after a detected forced password change) rather than treat as passing.

title: PUT /users/me accepts unbounded-length and control-character-laden firstName/lastName values
description: Unlike PUT /users/:id and POST / (both wrapped in validate([...nameValidators]) enforcing isLength({max:100}) and a NO_CONTROL_CHARS /^[^\x00-\x1F\x7F]*$/ pattern), PUT /me has zero express-validator middleware. A caller can submit an arbitrarily long name or one containing \r\n/other control bytes and have it persisted verbatim.
preconditions: Valid JWT for a seeded user
steps: Call PUT /users/me with firstName set to a 5,000-character string of repeated 'A's
Call PUT /users/me with firstName set to "Line1\r\nFAKE-LOG-ENTRY: admin granted"
expectedResult: Both requests currently succeed and persist the value as-is with no length cap or control-character stripping — a gap relative to the admin-edit path's defenses against oversized payloads and log/audit-trail forging via embedded control bytes.
